beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson eight. Fermentation and anaerobic respiration. [[loaf]]A lump of dough sits in a warm bowl, and slowly it swells into a loaf. Inside it are yeast cells, and the bubbles that puff it up are a clue about what they are doing. [[map]]Here is our respiration map once more. Most of it needs oxygen. [[gly]]But look at glycolysis, in the cytosol. [[cross]]It does not need oxygen at all, and today the mitochondrion is crossed out. What can a cell do when the oxygen runs out?
beats.need: [[gly]]Glycolysis turns one glucose into two pyruvate, and it nets two A T P, with or without oxygen. [[nad]]But look at what it uses along the way. Two N A D plus take up electrons and become two N A D H. [[stall]]A cell has only a small supply of N A D plus. If every one becomes N A D H, and none ever goes back, glycolysis runs out of its helper and stops. [[o2]]With oxygen, the chain hands those electrons to oxygen, and N A D plus comes back. [[no]]Without oxygen, the chain is stuck. So the cell needs some other way to turn N A D H back into N A D plus. [[two]]There are two answers: anaerobic respiration, and fermentation.
beats.anaero: [[chain]]In anaerobic respiration, the cell still runs an electron transport chain. But the last electron acceptor is not oxygen. [[sulfate]]In some bacteria it is sulfate. The chain still pumps protons, and chemiosmosis still makes A T P, so this is respiration, just with a different acceptor at the end. [[ferm]]Fermentation has no chain at all. [[sub]]The only A T P comes from glycolysis, by substrate-level phosphorylation, where an enzyme hands a phosphate straight to A D P. [[regen]]Fermentation is simply glycolysis, plus reactions that regenerate N A D plus, so that glycolysis can keep going. [[kinds]]There are two common kinds: alcohol fermentation, and lactic acid fermentation.
beats.alcohol: [[gly2]]Start with alcohol fermentation. Glycolysis makes two pyruvate and two A T P, and two N A D plus have become two N A D H. [[co2]]Now each pyruvate loses a carbon as carbon dioxide, and becomes acetaldehyde, a molecule with two carbons. [[red]]Then N A D H hands its electrons to the acetaldehyde, which is reduced to ethanol. [[regen2]]And that hands the cell its N A D plus back, ready for more glycolysis. [[count]]So per glucose: two pyruvate, two carbon dioxide, and two ethanol.
beats.yeast: [[yeast]]This is the work of yeast. The carbon dioxide puffs up bread dough and puts the bubbles in beer and sparkling wine, and the ethanol is the alcohol in them. Notice that the electrons end up on acetaldehyde, so acetaldehyde is the final acceptor here.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which step of alcohol fermentation releases carbon dioxide?
beats.lactic: [[gly3]]Lactic acid fermentation is simpler still. Glycolysis runs as before. [[direct]]This time, the electrons from N A D H go straight onto pyruvate. So pyruvate is reduced by N A D H, and becomes lactate. [[nocarbon]]No carbon dioxide is released, and there is no acetaldehyde step. [[regen3]]And again, N A D plus is regenerated, so glycolysis can continue.
beats.uses: [[cheese]]Some fungi and bacteria do this to make cheese and yogurt. [[muscle]]And so do your own muscle cells. When oxygen is scarce, in a hard sprint, a muscle fibre keeps making A T P this way, with lactate as the product. It is not a good long-term deal, as we are about to see.
beats.compare: [[side]]Put the two routes side by side. Both begin with glycolysis. [[acc]]In fermentation, the final electron acceptor is an organic molecule, pyruvate or acetaldehyde. In aerobic respiration it is oxygen. [[atp2]]Fermentation makes two A T P from one glucose. [[atp32]]Aerobic respiration makes about thirty to thirty-two. [[why]]The reason is simple. Fermentation stops after glycolysis, and so all the energy still locked in lactate and ethanol is never harvested. That is also why a fermenting cell must burn through far more glucose to get the same A T P. [[ten]]For example, to match one glucose's worth of respiration, a fermenting cell needs roughly fifteen glucose molecules, an estimate, not a slide figure.
beats.fork: [[fork]]Now we can read the fork. Glucose goes through glycolysis and becomes pyruvate in the cytosol. [[noo2]]With no oxygen, pyruvate goes to fermentation: ethanol, lactate, or other products. [[o2on]]With oxygen present, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion as acetyl co-A, and the citric acid cycle follows. [[obl]]Some organisms stay on one branch. Obligate anaerobes use only fermentation or anaerobic respiration, and they cannot survive in oxygen. [[fac]]Facultative anaerobes can use either branch. Yeast, and many bacteria, ferment when oxygen is missing and respire when it is there. [[sw]]They choose by what the environment offers.
beats.q2: Quick check. A yeast cell loses its oxygen. What does it do?
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Glycolysis makes A T P with or without oxygen, but it needs N A D plus. [[s2]]Fermentation regenerates N A D plus without a chain: alcohol fermentation makes ethanol and carbon dioxide, lactic acid fermentation makes lactate. [[s3]]It yields two A T P, against about thirty to thirty-two for respiration. [[s4]]Pyruvate is the fork, and oxygen decides the road. [[end]]Now try the practice.
